name: Nedim
bio: Ahmed Nedim was one of the most celebrated Ottoman poets of the early 18th century, the age later called the Tulip Era, a period of peace, luxury and garden-pavilion culture in Istanbul. He wrote the courtly ghazel and became librarian and boon-companion of the Grand Vezir Ibrahim Pasha.

He died in October 1730, when the palace was stormed in the uprising that overthrew Sultan Ahmed III. E. J. W. Gibb, whose History of Ottoman Poetry gives the first sustained English account of him, warned that Nedim's delicate verbal music could scarcely survive translation. The poems below are Gibb's renderings of ghazels from the fourth volume of that history.

poems.title: But a Glass or Two She Gave Us
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel in which the poet teases a wine-seller and his daughter with the promise of kisses, and the fair girl's wine is a cause of wild joy. Gibb's notes explain the proverbial phrase 'chewing mastic', meaning to promise something pleasant without saying what.

poems.title: Her Every Curl a Thousand Tangles Bears
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel praising the beloved's hair, eyes and manner, in which every curl and glance is a snare. Gibb's notes explain that her eyes speak of love more eloquently than a hundred thousand tongues.
poems.text:
Her every curl a thousand heart-enchanting tangles bears,
And every tangle in each curl a thousand souls ensnares.

A sly and roguish glance hath she, and a soft smile and sweet,
A dulcet and a graceful speech, and dear seductive airs.

Behold those locks of ambergris beneath her fez of white,
And see a wallflower sweet a vest of jasmine leaves that wears.

I may not tell the tale of her bright charms, nor mayst thou hear;
Yet naught but lack of some small troth her sweetest self impairs.

An eye she hath that knoweth many an hundred thousand tongues;
A thousand mates who understand its speech hath she for feres.

My lord, thou wert with envy torn, an if thou didst but know
What manner of adventure now Nedim in joyance shares.

poems.title: Yea, Her Fair and Lucent Neck
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel describing the beloved's neck, eyebrows and eyes, ending with the poet's own lovelorn sighs. Gibb's notes explain that the 'Primal Banquet' is a phrase borrowed from the mystic poets and used here conventionally.

poems.title: O My Wayward Fair
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel in which the beloved is compared to a rose and a cypress, and the poet cannot tell whether to take the bowl or the rose. Gibb's notes explain the wine and the bowl at the feast.
poems.text:
O my wayward fair, who thus hath reared thee sans all fear to be?
Who hath tendered thee that thus thou shamest e'en the cypress-tree?

Sweeter than all perfume, brighter than all bloom, thy dainty frame;
One would deem some rose had nursed thee in her bosom, love o' me.

Thou hast donned a rose-enwroughten rich brocade, but sore I fear
Lest the shadow of the broidered rose's thorn make thee to dree.

Holding in one hand a bowl, in one a rose, thou camest, sweet;
Ah, I knew not which thereof to take, the bowl, the rose, or thee.

Lo, there springs a jetting fountain from the Stream of Life, methought,
When thou lettest me that lovely lissom shape o' thine to see.

While the mirror of my bosom clear was as thy frame, alas,
For that even once I clipped thee not, thou darling fair and free.

Whensoe'er I ask it, saying: Who hath bowed thy body so?
Thee-ward ever points the beaker at the feast of mirth and glee.

poems.title: Thy Bosom Bright Hath Worked
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel praising the beloved's bosom, leg and navel, in the most daring imagery of the Ottoman love lyric. Gibb's notes explain that the delicate skin and the shift are regarded as great beauties.
poems.text:
Thy bosom bright hath worked the sun's pavilion dire dismay,
Thy leg diaphanous hath wrought the shaft of dawn's deray.

The vitals of the bud are torn with bitter pangs whene'er
Thy rose-like navel peepeth forth from 'neath thy shift, my may.

Astound thereat, with mouth agape, e'en like the slipper, bode
The cordwainer what time he saw thy lustrous ankle ray.

poems.title: Love-Distraught, My Heart and Soul
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel about the lover's ruin by the beloved's beauty, in which the lover calls her a 'Paynim' (infidel) in each couplet, a refrain of wounded affection.
poems.text:
Love-distraught, my heart and soul are gone for naught to beauties fair;
All my patience and endurance spent on torn and shredded spare.

Once I bared her lovely bosom, whereupon did calm and peace
Forth my breast take flight, but how I wist not, nay, nor why, nor where.

Paynim mole, and paynim tresses, paynim eyes, I cry ye grace;
All thy cruel beauty's kingdom is but Paynimrie, I swear.

Kisses on her neck and kisses on her bosom promised she;
Woe is me, for now the Paynim rues the troth she pledged while-ere.

Such the winsome grace wherewith she showed her locks 'neath her fez.
Whatsoever wight beheld her gazed bewildered then and there.

'Sorrowing for whom,' thou askest, 'weeps Nedim so passing sore?'
Ruthless, 'tis for thee that all men weep and wail in drear despair.

poems.title: Her Legs and Hips, Her Chin and Lips
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A wine-feast ghazel with a refrain on 'to mine own heart', in which the beloved is praised from head to foot and the poet asks the Sphere not to darken the feast.

poems.title: The Realm of Sufferance Thou'st Laid Waste
poems.author: Nedim
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel that calls the beloved 'Paynim' and compares her cruelty to that of Hulagu Khan, the Mongol conqueror whom Gibb's notes describe as a byword for a bloody tyrant.
poems.text:
The realm of sufferance thou'st laid waste; Hulagu Khan art hight, Paynim,
Have ruth! thou'st set the world aflame; art thou a burning light, Paynim?

A maiden's winsome air, thine air; a youthful gallant's tone, thy tone;
A torment thou! I wist not, art thou youth or maiden bright, Paynim?

What meaning bears that wede of flame-hued satin o'er thy shoulders thrown?
Art thou the soul-consuming gleam of grace and love-delight, Paynim?

Ah, what may be those secret, secret sighs, and what that rended spare?
Art thou, e'en thou, the wailing lover of some wanton wight, Paynim?

A many say to thee 'My Life;' another many say 'My Lore;'
What art thou? Art thou Life, or art thou Love? declare aright, Paynim.

The flame-hued wine hath flushed thee, dear, and set thy sweetest face aglow;
Art thou become the lamp wherewith the topers' circle is dight, Paynim?

O wherefore in the burnished mirror lookest thou so oft, my fair?
Art thou likewise astound of thine own dazzling beauty's sight, Paynim?

I've heard a Paynim hath made thrall of hapless and forlorn Nedim;
Art thou that foe unto the Faith, that adversary of right, Paynim?
